questions.q: How does PostgreSQL handle a new client connection, per this lesson?
options: It attaches the client directly to the shared memory area with no dedicated process
It queues the connection until a fixed thread pool has capacity
It assigns a worker thread inside a single shared process, like SQL Server
The postmaster forks a brand-new OS process, called a backend, dedicated to that connection
questions.explain: PostgreSQL is process-per-connection: the postmaster forks a dedicated backend OS process for each client, unlike SQL Server's thread-based model.

questions.q: Why is connection pooling closer to a requirement in PostgreSQL than in SQL Server, per this lesson?
options: SQL Server does not support connection pooling
PostgreSQL cannot handle more than a handful of connections at all
PostgreSQL has no way to close connections without restarting the server
Forking a new OS process per connection is heavier than spinning up a thread, making unpooled connections costlier at scale
questions.explain: Process-per-connection means each new connection costs more to set up than a thread would, which is why tools like PgBouncer are standard in PostgreSQL deployments.

questions.q: What is the role of the autovacuum launcher, per this lesson?
options: It flushes shared_buffers pages directly to the network
It compiles query execution plans
It starts autovacuum worker processes that reclaim space from dead rows
It handles all client authentication
questions.explain: The autovacuum launcher is one of the postmaster's supervised background processes, started to reclaim space left behind by PostgreSQL's MVCC model.

questions.q: How does work_mem behave, per this lesson?
options: It only applies to VACUUM and CREATE INDEX operations
It has no effect on query execution
It is a single global cap shared across the entire server at all times
It is a per-operation budget — a single complex query can use several multiples of it across its sorts and hashes
questions.explain: work_mem applies per sort or hash operation, so a query with several such operations can use multiples of the configured value simultaneously.

questions.q: Why is shared_buffers typically sized much smaller relative to total RAM than SQL Server's buffer pool, per this lesson?
options: PostgreSQL also relies heavily on the operating system's own file-system cache, creating a double-caching layout
PostgreSQL cannot use more than a fixed small amount of memory under any circumstances
shared_buffers is not actually used for caching table or index pages
SQL Server does not use any operating system caching at all
questions.explain: A common PostgreSQL guideline sizes shared_buffers around 25% of system RAM because the OS file cache also does real caching work, unlike SQL Server's model.
